claims.text: Oxidation resistance in high-temperature MPEAs is governed by formation of stable, adherent surface oxide layers.
Material integrity in high-temperature MPEAs is governed by formation of stable, adherent surface oxide layers.
Specific alloying elements facilitate protective oxide formation by promoting selective oxidation.
Specific alloying elements suppress internal oxidation.
Aluminum and chromium are examples of alloying elements that promote selective oxidation.
The controlled comparison varies aluminum and chromium concentrations while keeping other compositional factors constant.
The proposed exposure condition is air at 1000°C for 100 hours.
Increasing selective-oxidation-promoting elements causes formation of a stable, adherent surface oxide layer.
Selective oxidation of alloying elements forms protective oxide layers.
Protective oxide layers act as barriers to further oxidation.
Protective oxide layers prevent degradation of the underlying alloy.
Suppressing internal oxidation preserves material integrity.
MPEAs with higher concentrations of selective-oxidation-promoting elements will show lower oxidation mass gain than the low-concentration baseline.
MPEAs with higher concentrations of selective-oxidation-promoting elements will show less internal oxidation than the baseline.
MPEAs with higher concentrations of selective-oxidation-promoting elements will retain mechanical properties better than the baseline.
The hypothesis applies only to MPEA compositions that permit selective oxidation.
The hypothesis applies between the temperature threshold for significant oxidation and the alloy melting point.
Synergistic interactions among selective-oxidation-promoting elements in multiprincipal-element systems are not fully understood.
